title: Config Propagation Delay
summary: Compute how long a config push takes to reach every service in a weighted network.

stages.title: Time to reach every service
stages.requirement:
Services are numbered `0..n-1`. A config push starts at `source` at time 0. Each link
`(a, b, ms)` means service `a` forwards the config to `b`, arriving `ms` milliseconds later.
Links are **one-directional** and `ms >= 0`. A service forwards immediately on receipt.

Write `propagation_delay(n, links, source)` returning the time when the **last** service
receives the config, or `-1` if some service is unreachable.

```python
propagation_delay(4, [(0, 1, 5), (0, 2, 1), (2, 1, 2), (1, 3, 1)], 0)  # -> 4
# 0 -> 2 (1ms) -> 1 (3ms) -> 3 (4ms)
```

Up to 20,000 services and 100,000 links. There may be several links between the same pair.

hiddenTests.name: test_longer_path_with_fewer_ms
hiddenTests.description: Fewest hops is not fastest: BFS gets this wrong.

hiddenTests.name: test_large_grid
hiddenTests.code:
def test_large_grid():
    n = 20_000
    links = [(i, i + 1, 1) for i in range(n - 1)] + [(0, i, n) for i in range(1, n)]
    assert propagation_delay(n, links, 0) == n - 1

hints: Unweighted BFS counts hops, not milliseconds. Which algorithm finds shortest weighted paths with non-negative weights?
Dijkstra: pop the service with the smallest known arrival time from a min-heap and relax its outgoing links.
Skip stale heap entries (time greater than the best known). The answer is the max over all arrival times, or -1 if any is unreached.

solution.explanation:
This is single-source shortest paths with non-negative weights, so Dijkstra's algorithm
fits. With a binary heap and lazy deletion (skipping popped entries that are worse than
the recorded best), each link is relaxed once. The time the last service hears about
the config is the maximum shortest-path distance.
